title: Hypersweep latency variance lab notes — mixed-seq stress experiments
content:
Context:
This was a focused lab session to reproduce and triage intermittent p99 spikes observed in recent mixed-sequence shadow runs. The spike is most visible when workload mix includes a small fraction (~5%) of long-sequence (>1024 tokens) requests interleaved with many short requests. We ran a hypersweep over kv-cache settings, batch sizes, and kernel-selection flags to isolate the source.

Meeting / lab details:
- Date: 2026-06-15
- Lab duration: 09:00-12:30 PT
- Environment: staging-gpu-pool-7 (A100), runtime-build: v0.68.3-hypersweep, model-variant: gpt-open-8b-qa-v1
- Workload generator: benchgen v2.1 (mixed-seq profile: 90% 32 tokens, 5% 256 tokens, 5% 2048 tokens), target QPS: 180
- Orchestrator: local-runner + shadow routing to shadow-alloc-3

Attendees:
Aisha Patel (owner), Marco Li, Diego Romero, Priya Shah, Samir Khan (SRE), + Slack observers from product-hosted-api

Agenda:
1) Review recent regression traces (JIRA-10934)
2) Run controlled hypersweep (kv-cache: on/off; cache-cap: 1GB/4GB; eviction-policy: LRU/temperature)
3) Kernel flags: use-optimized-attn true/false, fp16-accel true/false
4) Capture traces, per-thread CPU, GPU timelines, and network IO
5) Document any reproducible patterns and next steps

Summary of experiments run (swept parameters):
- Sweep matrix: 3 (kv-cache size) x 2 (kv-cache on/off) x 2 (eviction policy) x 2 (optimized-attn) x 2 (fp16-accel) = 48 runs, each 15m stable window
- Collected: qps, p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, GPU utilization, PCIe memcpy counters, CPU steal, and perf traces
- Run ids: bench-20260615-01 through bench-20260615-48 (see linked CI job for raw logs)

Key observations (most reproducible):
1) p99 spike correlates with "kv-cache on" + small cache-cap (1GB) + long-seq presence. When cache fills and we evict frequently, p99 increases by 2.6x compared to baseline (cache off or cache large).
   - Example: baseline (cache off): p99=180ms; kv-cache small: p99=480ms at same qps.
2) Spikes align with a burst of PCIe memcpy activity on GPU0 (captured in nvprof/trace windows). The memcpy bursts occur when large kv-cache entries are evicted and then long-seq requests require reloading large KV blocks.
3) Enabling optimized-attn reduced p50/p95 marginally but did not eliminate p99 spikes; kernel selection added a short (5-15ms) overhead per token for long sequences in some runs.
4) fp16-accel trades some tail stability for throughput; with fp16 on we observe slightly higher variance in p99 during eviction events (suspected due to extra validation/format conversion paths in runtime code).
5) Eviction policy jitter: LRU produced more frequent small memcpy spikes; temperature-based eviction produced fewer, larger spikes. Temperature-based with larger cache-cap produced best overall tail profile.

Diagnostic traces / artifacts notes:
- Trace excerpt (bench-20260615-12): timeline shows request A (short) -> request B (long) starts at t=3.2s; at t=3.21s we observe kv-evict(0x7f..) followed by memcpy(2.3MB) -> memcpy stalls main serving thread for ~8ms; aggregated across concurrent requests this causes p99 amplification.
- GPU metrics: GPU utilization steady (~64%) except during memcpy bursts where compute drops to ~12% for ~10-30ms.
- CPU: one core saturates during eviction callbacks (python GC spikes pinned to eviction handler).

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Eviction-induced memcpy to/from host is the primary driver of p99 spikes when small cache-cap + mixed long sequences present. Memory traffic blocks compute and stalls other requests in the same worker.
B) Eviction handler runs on main serving thread (or a hot path) causing CPU-side stalls that backpressure the request queue.
C) Kernel-selection path for long sequences triggers a block copy fallback that is slower in fp16+optimized-attn interplay.

Quick reproducer command (lab):
- benchgen --profile mixed-seq --qps 180 --duration 900 --model gpt-open-8b-qa-v1 --kv-cache on --kv-cache-cap 1GB --eviction lru --flags use-optimized-attn=true,fp16-accel=true

Immediate mitigations tested during the lab:
- Increase kv-cache-cap to 4GB: eliminated most mid-run evictions, p99 reduced to ~220ms (still ~20ms above baseline).
- Move eviction callbacks to background worker thread (local patch): reduced CPU-side GC spikes; p99 improved by ~30% in patched runs (bench-20260615-33/34).
- Throttle long-seq injection rate in generator to 1%: p99 approaches baseline; confirms sensitivity to long-seq fraction.

Action items and owners:
- Aisha: Draft follow-up PR to make eviction handler asynchronous and add metrics for memcpy bytes and eviction counts per worker (target PR by 2026-06-18). Linked PR draft: github PR 1248.
- Marco: Run additional hypersweep with on-host pinned DMA buffers to measure memcpy overhead without CPU involvement (due 2026-06-17).
- Diego: Profile kernel selection codepath and add instrumentation for fallback copy vs zero-copy to confirm hypothesis C (due 2026-06-19).
- Priya: Add synthetic test to CI that injects 2% long-seq requests to catch regressions in p99 (due 2026-06-22).
- Samir: Validate SLOs for dedicated pools and draft SRE runbook entry for eviction-induced stalls (due 2026-06-20).

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we prefer larger default kv-cache-cap on hosted for mixed workloads at cost of memory footprint? (Product tradeoff)
- Should eviction callbacks be moved out-of-process entirely (cost/complexity)?
- Is there a quick kernel-level optimization for long-seq path to avoid extra copies when fp16-accel is enabled?

Notes / misc:
- This lab produced a reliable repro within our staging pool; we should schedule a short shadow run on prod-dedicated with the async-evict patch before rolling to all customers.
- Observers from hosted-api suggested flagging long-seq customers to the routing policy (route long sequences to pools with larger cache capacity) as an immediate policy mitigation.

References:
- bench run logs: https://ci.internal.redwood/jobs/bench-20260615-raw (see bench-20260615-12,33,34)
- JIRA ticket: JIRA-10934 (investigations + traces attached)

Next sync: 2026-06-18 10:00 PT (sync to review PRs and additional sweep results)

End of notes.
